{{Short description|Mathematical constant}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Golomb–Dickman constant''', named after [[Solomon W. Golomb]] and [[Karl Dickman]], is a [[mathematical constant]], which arises in the theory of [[random permutation]]s and in [[number theory]]. Its value is

:<math>\lambda = 0.62432 99885 43550 87099 29363 83100 83724\dots</math> {{OEIS|A084945}}

It is not known whether this constant is rational or irrational.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lagarias|first1=Jeffrey|title=Euler's constant: Euler's work and modern developments|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.|volume=50|issue=4|pages=527–628|year=2013|arxiv=1303.1856|doi=10.1090/S0273-0979-2013-01423-X|bibcode=2013arXiv1303.1856L|s2cid=119612431}}</ref>

Its [[simple continued fraction]] is given by <math>[0; 1, 1, 1, 1, 1,  22, 1, 2, 3, 1, ...]</math>, which appears to have an unusually large number of 1s.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Golomb-Dickman Constant Continued Fraction |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Golomb-DickmanConstantContinuedFraction.html |access-date=2024-10-11 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref>

== Definitions ==
Let ''a''<sub>''n''</sub> be the average &mdash; taken over all [[permutation]]s of a set of size ''n'' &mdash; of the length of the longest [[cyclic permutation|cycle]] in each permutation.  Then the Golomb–Dickman constant is

: <math>\lambda = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{a_n}{n}.</math>

In the language of [[probability theory]], <math>\lambda n</math> is asymptotically the [[expected value|expected]] length of the longest cycle in a [[discrete uniform distribution|uniformly distributed]] [[random permutation]] of a set of size ''n''.

In number theory, the Golomb–Dickman constant appears in connection with the average size of the largest [[prime factor]] of an integer. More precisely,
:<math>\lambda = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n \sum_{k=2}^n \frac{\log(P_1(k))}{\log(k)},</math>
where <math>P_1(k)</math> is the largest prime factor of ''k'' {{OEIS|A006530}}. So if ''k'' is a ''d'' digit integer, then <math>\lambda d</math> is the asymptotic average number of digits of the largest [[prime factor]] of ''k''.

The Golomb–Dickman constant appears in number theory in a different way.   What is the probability that second largest prime factor of ''n'' is smaller than the square root of the largest prime factor of ''n''?  Asymptotically, this probability is <math>\lambda</math>.
More precisely,
:<math>\lambda = \lim_{n\to\infty} \text{Prob}\left\{P_2(n) \le \sqrt{P_1(n)}\right\}</math>
where <math>P_2(n)</math> is the second largest prime factor ''n''.

The Golomb–Dickman constant also arises when we consider the average length of the largest cycle of any function from a finite set to itself.   If ''X'' is a finite set, if we repeatedly apply a function ''f'': ''X'' &rarr; ''X'' to any element ''x'' of this set, it eventually enters a cycle, meaning that for some ''k'' we have <math>f^{n+k}(x) = f^n(x)</math> for sufficiently large ''n''; the smallest ''k'' with this property is the length of the cycle. Let ''b''<sub>''n''</sub> be the average, taken over all functions from a set of size ''n'' to itself, of the length of the largest cycle.  Then Purdom and Williams<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Purdon|first1=P.|last2=Williams|first2=J.H|title=Cycle length in a random function|journal=Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.|volume=133|issue=2|pages=547–551|year=1968|doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1968-0228032-3|doi-access=free}}</ref> proved that

: <math>   \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{b_n}{\sqrt{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2} } \lambda. </math>

== Formulas ==

There are several expressions for <math>\lambda</math>.  These include:<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Golomb-Dickman Constant |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Golomb-DickmanConstant.html |access-date=2024-10-11 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref>

:<math>\lambda = \int_0^1 e^{\mathrm{li}(t)} \, dt </math>

where <math>\mathrm{li}(t)</math> is the [[logarithmic integral]],

:<math>\lambda = \int_0^\infty e^{-t - E_1(t)} \, dt </math>

where <math>E_1(t)</math> is the [[exponential integral]], and

:<math>\lambda = \int_0^\infty \frac{\rho(t)}{t+2} \, dt </math>

and

:<math>\lambda = \int_0^\infty \frac{\rho(t)}{(t+1)^2} \, dt </math>

where <math>\rho(t)</math> is the [[Dickman–de Bruijn function|Dickman function]].
